metadata.title: Socioeconomic Status and Academic Achievement in Primary and Secondary Education: a Meta-analytic Review

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This article is a meta-analytic review combining (i) correlations extracted from 326 empirical studies and (ii) correlations computed from three international large-scale assessments (PISA, TIMSS, PIRLS) using the IEA International Database Analyzer (IDA). Because the analysis is conducted at the level of effect sizes/country-level correlations rather than re-estimating achievement models from raw microdata, the paper does not report the use of student sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures in the meta-analytic stage. For the ILSA component, the authors state that IDA was used to “seamlessly take into account sampling information and multiple imputed achievement scores,” implying that the ILSA complex survey design and imputation were handled within IDA when computing correlations. Analysts using the same ILSA databases should apply the official ILSA sampling weights and replicate-weight variance estimation (as provided in the international database tools) when recomputing achievement–SES correlations, and should ensure that plausible-value imputation is handled consistently with the ILSA scoring procedures.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable to this extraction because the paper is a meta-analysis that aggregates correlation effect sizes rather than training predictive models on PV-based achievement scores. For the ILSA component, the authors state that IDA was used to account for multiple imputed achievement scores when computing correlations, but the paper does not report a specific PV-combining rule (e.g., Rubin’s rules) at the meta-analytic level. Missing-data handling is not reported because the study does not describe an imputation/deletion strategy for missingness in the aggregated effect-size dataset; instead, it relies on the original studies’ reported correlations and IDA’s internal handling for the ILSA computations.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: This is a meta-analytic review rather than a single empirical ML training study. For the empirical-studies meta-analysis, inclusion required: (a) at least one correlation (r) between SES and academic achievement, (b) typically developing students in primary-to-secondary education, (c) individual-level r, (d) studies conducted 1990–Dec 2021, (e) published or unpublished in English, and (f) exclusion of disability-only samples, pre-primary/college samples, and longitudinal designs where SES was measured after achievement. To avoid redundancy between the two meta-analyses, 25 empirical studies (59 effect sizes) using PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS were excluded from the empirical-studies meta-analysis. For the ILSA-based meta-analysis, the authors used PISA (2000–2018), TIMSS (1995–2019), and PIRLS (2001–2016) and computed SES–achievement correlations at the country/area level using IDA, treating countries/areas as the unit of analysis; they also applied indicator-specific rules to avoid overlap (e.g., using overall SES indicators rather than sub-indicators when both were available, and using student-reported data when both parent and student data were available for the same indicator).

Across both components, the overall SES–academic achievement association is moderate (empirical studies: r = 0.22, 95% CI [0.20, 0.23]; ILSAs: r = 0.28, 95% CI [0.28, 0.29]). Moderation analyses show that the SES–achievement relation strengthened over time (empirical: Years2 vs Years1 β = 0.05, p = 0.04; ILSAs: Years3 vs Years1 β = 0.06, p < 0.001) and that educational expansion indicators (net enrollment ratio; duration of compulsory education) were associated with stronger SES–achievement correlations in the ILSA meta-analysis. The authors emphasize correlational evidence and caution against causal interpretation, and they argue that educational equity policies should prioritize quality alongside access. data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is a meta-analytic review rather than an empirical machine-learning study. As a result, there is no single student-level ML pipeline, no PV-handling choice for a predictive model, no missing-data strategy for an ML dataset, and no per-country sample-size table extracted from the provided text. The ILSA component uses IDA to compute correlations while accounting for sampling and multiple imputed achievement scores, but the paper does not provide the country-by-country n needed to populate the countries array with ISO codes and per-country sample sizes.
